rows.selection_reason: With no experiments completed, the highest-priority uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline and determining whether RNA alone carries sufficient signal. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal, interpretable configuration: a standard linear dimensionality reduction on a single RNA profile with no learned encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. It serves as the reference floor against which all RNA-encoder choices (scvi, scgpt), profile settings (multiprofile), and multimodal combinations will be compared. Because PCA is computationally cheap, it also uses the experiment budget efficiently, freeing resources for subsequent, more complex runs. If config_001 yields strong accuracy, it confirms RNA is informative and motivates exploring better encoders or multimodal fusion next; if it is weak, it signals that the image modality or learned RNA encoders are critical, redirecting the search. No other single experiment reduces as much downstream uncertainty per unit of compute in the first step.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding 48.5% accuracy / 46.4% F1 — a very weak baseline with no information about whether the image modality, better encoders, or multiprofile aggregation contribute. Question being tested: Does adding the image modality (resnet50, concat fusion) to the existing RNA baseline improve performance? This is the most fundamental design question for a multimodal cellular profiling study. Why this is the best next experiment: config_016 is the minimal, cleanest extension of config_001 — same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), same profile setting (singleprofile), simply adding resnet50 image features with the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the effect of modality addition with minimal confounds. If multimodal outperforms the RNA-only baseline, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies subsequent investment in better encoders/fusion. If it does not, it signals that the bottleneck lies in representation quality (RNA or image encoder) rather than modality combination, redirecting the search efficiently. Under a tight budget, resolving this binary question is more informative than, e.g., testing a different RNA encoder in isolation, because it determines the entire architecture of subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA, ResNet50, concat) outperformed config_001 (RNA-only PCA) by ~4.2% accuracy, confirming that adding an image branch with concat fusion is beneficial. Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet on whether multiprofile (aggregating multiple cell profiles per sample) improves over singleprofile in the multimodal setting. This is a fundamental architectural decision that, if positive, would unlock a large subset of configurations and potentially yield further gains. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the most direct logical extension of the best-performing config_016, changing only the profile setting (single→multi) and adding the corresponding avgpool aggregation while keeping fusion=concat fixed. This isolates the multiprofile/aggregation question as the primary new variable. Under a limited budget, resolving whether multiprofile helps is more informative than testing minor fusion variants (e.g., weighted vs concat) because it determines whether an entire axis of the search space is worth further exploration.

Evidence: The current best (config_018, acc=0.619) shows that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation in a multimodal setting is a strong direction, with a large gain over singleprofile (+0.092). Uncertainty: We have only tested avgpool aggregation in the multiprofile setting; it is unclear whether a transformer-based aggregation could capture more complex inter-profile relationships and yield further gains. This experiment (config_020) changes exactly one variable from config_018—aggregation from avgpool to transformer—while holding multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, and concat fusion constant. This isolates the effect of aggregation sophistication. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly exploits the most promising configuration while resolving a key design question: whether the simple average is already near-optimal or whether learned (transformer) aggregation offers meaningful additional signal, which would redirect subsequent experiments toward transformer-based variants.

The current best (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.619) has only been tested with concat fusion. Config_019 is identical in every respect except fusion=weighted, making it a clean single-variable A/B test. This directly resolves whether the fusion mechanism (learned weighted combination vs. simple concatenation) is an important design axis. If weighted fusion improves performance, it validates a whole family of configurations (e.g., with ViT-L or scGPT) and suggests the modality combination strategy matters. If it does not, we can rule out weighted fusion and redirect remaining budget toward image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA encoder (scGPT/scVI) variations. Given the limited budget, isolating this binary design question with the highest-performing pipeline already identified is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). We have strong evidence that multiprofile+avgpool+weighted is the best combination of profile/aggregation/fusion settings, but the image encoder has only been tested as resnet50. Uncertainty: Whether upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a substantially larger, transformer-based architecture) yields meaningful gains in the multimodal setting. This experiment (config_025) is a clean single-variable swap—changing only the image encoder while holding all other parameters at their best-known values—making the result directly interpretable. It is the best use of the next budget slot because the image encoder is the largest untested architectural dimension, likely to have the highest potential impact on performance, and testing it at the current best configuration maximizes both expected performance and information gain about whether further investment in image representation is warranted.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all completed multimodal experiments share this encoder. The dominant design decisions (multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) are well-established, but the RNA encoder is the largest untested variable. Question: Does replacing PCA with scvi_n200 (a learned, biologically-informed latent representation) improve performance when all other settings match the current best? Why this experiment: config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable ablation against config_019, isolating the RNA encoder effect. This is the highest-information next step because the RNA encoder has the largest remaining uncertainty—if scvi_n200 helps, it opens a productive exploitation path (scgpt, etc.); if it does not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget to other dimensions. It avoids the smaller, already-nearly-resolved image-encoder question (resnet50 vs ViT-L differ by only ~0.4%).

Evidence: The strongest finding so far is that scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA for the RNA encoder (config_031: 0.678 vs config_019: 0.639, a ~4-point gain), while other design choices (avgpool over transformer, weighted over concat, ResNet50 ≈ ViT-L) show smaller, more settled effects. The RNA encoder remains the largest unexplored lever: scgpt has not been tested in any context. Question: config_043 (scgpt, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable swap from the current best (config_031), changing only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt. This directly tests whether a generative-model-based RNA encoder can surpass the VAE-based scvi_n200, or whether scvi_n200's learned latent space is already near-optimal for downstream classification. Why this is the best next experiment: it targets the dimension with the highest remaining uncertainty and the largest potential upside, keeps all other factors at their empirically best values for a clean attribution, and avoids re-testing dimensions (aggregation, fusion, image encoder) where evidence already points in a clear direction. Under a limited budget, resolving the RNA-encoder question is more informative than marginal refinements to already-settled choices.

Evidence: The current best is config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at acc=0.678. With pca_n2000, resnet50 and vit_l performed nearly identically (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a weaker RNA encoder. Question: Does swapping resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l with the superior scvi_n200 encoder yield a meaningful gain, confirming the image encoder is not a bottleneck, or does resnet50 interact favorably with scvi_n200 in a way vit_l does not? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable change from the current best configuration, directly testing whether the image encoder choice can still be improved. If vit_l matches or exceeds resnet50, it validates the current architecture and frees the next experiment to explore other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation with scvi_n200). If resnet50 clearly wins, it confirms we've locked in the optimal image encoder and the remaining budget should focus on other design choices. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.7062 acc. The two remaining untested design axes for this strongest encoder pair are aggregation (transformer) and fusion (concat). Aggregation has shown the larger historical effect (avgpool beat transformer by ~4-6 pp with PCA+ResNet50), so testing whether that ordering holds with the best encoders is the higher-value question. Config_039 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) isolates the aggregation variable while keeping the best fusion (weighted) fixed. If transformer underperforms avgpool again, it confirms avgpool is robustly superior across encoder quality levels and we can lock that choice; if it matches or exceeds config_037, it reveals that stronger encoders change the aggregation dynamics. This is the most informative single experiment for reducing uncertainty about the aggregation design decision in the region of the search space where performance is highest.
